stacks.name: Web Foundations
stacks.description: How the internet and browsers actually work, before writing a single line of code.

lessons.title: Clients, servers and how a page reaches you

content.objective: Understand what happens between typing a URL and seeing a page.

sections.heading: The web is a conversation
sections.body:
The web is millions of computers talking to each other. Your device (the **client**) asks for things; other computers (**servers**) answer. When you type `example.com` and press Enter, your browser sends a **request** and the server sends back a **response** — usually an HTML document.

This request/response exchange follows a set of rules called **HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol). Think of it as the grammar both sides agree to speak.

sections.heading: URLs: addresses for everything
sections.body:
A URL has parts, each with a job:

- `https://` — the **scheme**: which protocol to use (`https` is HTTP with encryption).
- `www.example.com` — the **domain**: a human-friendly name for a server.
- `/products/shoes` — the **path**: which resource on that server.
- `?color=red` — the **query string**: extra parameters.

Computers don't actually use names — they use numeric **IP addresses** like `93.184.216.34`. The **DNS** system is the phone book that converts `example.com` into an IP address before the request is sent.

sections.heading: What comes back
sections.body: The server responds with a **status code** (`200` = OK, `404` = not found, `500` = server error) and a **body** — the HTML for the page. The browser then reads the HTML, discovers it also needs CSS files, images and JavaScript, and fires off more requests for each. A single page view is often 30-100 requests.

sections.heading: Frontend vs backend
sections.body: **Frontend** is everything that runs in the browser: HTML (structure), CSS (appearance), JavaScript (behavior). **Backend** is everything that runs on the server: databases, authentication, business logic. As a frontend developer you build the client side — but you constantly talk to backends through HTTP.

keyTakeaways: The browser (client) requests, the server responds — over HTTP.
DNS turns domain names into IP addresses.
Status codes summarize what happened: 200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error.
Frontend = HTML + CSS + JavaScript running in the browser.

content.objective: Verify you can explain the request/response cycle.

questions.prompt: What does DNS do?

Converts domain names into IP addresses
questions.explanation: DNS is the lookup system that maps human-friendly names like example.com to numeric IP addresses.

questions.prompt: Your browser receives a 404 status code. What does it mean?
options: The requested resource was not found
questions.explanation: 4xx codes are client-side errors; 404 specifically means the resource doesn't exist at that path.

questions.prompt: Which of these runs in the browser?
options: JavaScript that opens a dropdown menu
questions.explanation: Frontend code (HTML/CSS/JS) runs in the browser; databases and sensitive logic live on servers.

questions.prompt: What is HTTPS?
questions.explanation: The S stands for Secure — the same protocol wrapped in TLS encryption so others can't read the traffic.

skills.title: How Browsers Turn Code into Pixels

lessons.title: The rendering pipeline in plain language

content.objective: Know what the browser does with HTML, CSS and JS — so later debugging makes sense.

sections.heading: Three languages, three jobs
sections.body:
- **HTML** describes *what things are*: a heading, a paragraph, a button.
- **CSS** describes *what things look like*: colors, sizes, positions.
- **JavaScript** describes *what things do*: respond to clicks, fetch data, update the page.

A useful analogy: HTML is the skeleton, CSS is the skin and clothes, JavaScript is the muscles.

sections.heading: From text file to picture
sections.body:
When HTML arrives, the browser parses it into a tree of objects called the **DOM** (Document Object Model) — every tag becomes a node. CSS is parsed into its own tree, then combined with the DOM to compute the final style of every element. The browser then calculates **layout** (where everything goes and how big it is) and finally **paints** pixels to the screen.

JavaScript can reach into the DOM at any time and change it — add nodes, remove them, edit text — and the browser re-renders what changed. This is the foundation of every interactive site you have ever used.

sections.heading: DevTools: your X-ray glasses
sections.body: Every modern browser ships with Developer Tools (right-click any page → *Inspect*). The **Elements** panel shows the live DOM and lets you edit styles on the fly. The **Console** shows JavaScript output and errors. The **Network** panel lists every request the page made. You will live in these panels — open them now on any website and change something's color just to prove you can.

keyTakeaways: HTML → DOM tree; CSS styles it; layout and paint turn it into pixels.
JavaScript edits the DOM and the browser re-renders.
DevTools (Inspect) is the single most important learning tool you have.

content.objective: Set up the minimal toolkit: a code editor, a project folder, and a save-refresh loop.

sections.heading: The only three tools you need
sections.body:
1. **A code editor** — VS Code is the standard: free, fast, great extensions.
2. **A browser** — Chrome, Edge or Firefox, for viewing pages and DevTools.
3. **A project folder** — a plain folder on your computer where your files live.

That's it. No frameworks, no installs beyond the editor. A website at its core is just text files.

sections.heading: The save-refresh loop
sections.body:
Your entire workflow for the next several weeks:

1. Edit a file in your editor.
2. Save it (Ctrl/Cmd + S).
3. Refresh the browser tab (Ctrl/Cmd + R).
4. See the change.

Tip: install the *Live Server* extension in VS Code — it auto-refreshes the browser every time you save, removing step 3.

sections.heading: File naming habits that save pain
sections.body: Use lowercase file names without spaces: `about-me.html`, not `About Me.HTML`. The homepage of a site is conventionally named `index.html` — servers serve it automatically when someone visits the folder. Keep images in an `images/` subfolder and styles in `styles/` once projects grow.

keyTakeaways: A website is text files; the editor writes them, the browser renders them.
index.html is the conventional homepage name.
Lowercase, hyphenated file names prevent broken links later.

sections.body:
HTML is made of **elements**. Most have an opening tag, content, and a closing tag: `

Hello there

` - `

` — opening tag (p = paragraph) - `Hello there` — content - `

` — closing tag (note the slash) Some elements are **void** — they have no content and no closing tag: ``, `
`, ``. Elements can also carry **attributes**, name-value pairs inside the opening tag:

sections.heading: The boilerplate every page needs
sections.body: Every HTML document follows the same skeleton:

code.snippet:
Hello, world!

This is my very first webpage.

sections.heading: What each line does
sections.body:
- `<!DOCTYPE html>` tells the browser: this is modern HTML.
- `<html lang="en">` wraps everything; `lang` helps screen readers and search engines.
- `<head>` holds information *about* the page — nothing here is visible.
- `<meta charset="UTF-8">` enables all characters and emoji.
- The viewport meta makes the page scale correctly on phones.
- `<title>` is the text in the browser tab.
- `<body>` holds everything the user actually sees.

sections.heading: Nesting rules
sections.body:
Elements nest like boxes inside boxes — the inner one must close before the outer one: ✅ `

This is important text

` ❌ `

This is important

` Indent nested elements by two spaces so the structure stays readable. The browser forgives many mistakes, but sloppy nesting causes bugs that are miserable to find later.

keyTakeaways: Elements = opening tag + content + closing tag; void elements have neither.
head = information about the page; body = visible content.
Always close inner elements before outer ones.

content.objective: Structure whole pages with landmark elements instead of anonymous divs.

sections.heading: Why semantics beat div soup
sections.body: You *could* build a page from nothing but `<div>` boxes — but a div says nothing about what it contains. Semantic landmarks describe the page's regions, so screen-reader users can jump straight to navigation or main content, and search engines understand your layout:

code.snippet:
Trailhead Coffee

  • Home
  • Menu
  • Contact

We roast on Tuesdays

Fresh beans every week...

Opening hours

Mon–Sat, 8–18

© 2026 Trailhead Coffee

sections.heading: When to use which
sections.body:
- `<header>` — intro content: logo, site title, nav.
- `<nav>` — a block of major navigation links.
- `<main>` — the unique content of *this* page; exactly one per page.
- `<article>` — self-contained content that would make sense on its own (a post, a product card).
- `<section>` — a thematic grouping with a heading.
- `<aside>` — tangential content: sidebars, related links.
- `<footer>` — copyright, secondary links.
- `<div>` — still fine! But only as a styling hook when no semantic element fits.

keyTakeaways: Landmarks let assistive tech and search engines navigate your page.
Exactly one main per page.
Reach for div only when nothing semantic fits.

content.objective: Build forms users can actually fill out — with keyboard, screen reader or mouse.

sections.heading: The form skeleton
sections.body: A form groups controls and defines where the data goes:

code.snippet:
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

sections.heading: Labels are non-negotiable
sections.body: Every input needs a `<label>` whose `for` attribute matches the input's `id`. This makes the label clickable, tells screen readers what the field is, and enlarges the touch target on phones. Placeholder text is **not** a substitute — it vanishes when typing starts.

sections.heading: Input types do work for you
sections.body: `type="email"` validates the format and shows the @ keyboard on phones. Other useful types: `password`, `number`, `date`, `checkbox`, `radio`, `tel`, `url`. Radios sharing the same `name` become a choose-one group:

code.snippet:
<fieldset>
  <legend>Roast preference</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="roast" value="light"> Light</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="roast" value="dark"> Dark</label>
</fieldset>

sections.heading: Free validation
sections.body: Attributes give you validation with zero JavaScript: `required`, `minlength`, `maxlength`, `min`, `max`, and `pattern` for regex checks. The browser blocks submission and shows a message automatically. Custom, prettier validation can come later with JS — but native validation should always be the baseline.

keyTakeaways: Every input gets a label linked via for/id.
Input types unlock validation and better mobile keyboards.
fieldset + legend group related controls like radio sets.

content.objective: Write CSS rules and predict which one wins when they conflict.

sections.heading: Your first stylesheet
sections.body: CSS lives in a .css file linked from the head:

code.snippet:
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles/main.css">
</head>

sections.heading: Anatomy of a rule
sections.body: A rule has a **selector** (who to style) and **declarations** (what to change):

sections.heading: Classes are your workhorse
sections.body: Element selectors (`h1`) style *every* such element. Classes (`.card`) style opt-in groups — this is what you'll use most. IDs (`#site-logo`) are unique per page and very strong; prefer classes for styling and save ids for form labels and link anchors.

sections.heading: The cascade: who wins?
sections.body:
When two rules target the same element, the browser resolves conflicts by:
1. **Specificity** — id beats class beats element. `.card p` (class+element) beats `p`.
2. **Source order** — with equal specificity, the *later* rule wins.

Keep specificity low and consistent (mostly single classes) and the cascade stays predictable instead of becoming a fight.

keyTakeaways: Rule = selector + declarations; classes are the default tool.
Specificity: id > class > element; ties go to the later rule.
:hover and friends style element states.

content.objective: Control spacing and sizing deliberately instead of nudging numbers until it looks right.

sections.heading: The four layers
sections.body: Every element is a rectangular box with four layers, inside-out: **content → padding → border → margin**. Padding is space *inside* the border (gets the background color); margin is space *outside* it (transparent, pushes neighbors away).

sections.heading: box-sizing: the sanity setting
sections.body: By default, width applies to the content only — padding and border are added *on top*, so a 300px card with 20px padding is actually 340px wide. Every real project fixes this globally:

sections.heading: display: block, inline, inline-block
sections.body:
- **block** elements (div, p, h1, section) take the full width and stack vertically.
- **inline** elements (a, strong, span) flow within text and ignore width/height.
- **inline-block** flows like text but accepts width, height and vertical padding — handy for button-like links.

sections.heading: position: escaping normal flow
sections.body:
- `position: relative` — nudge an element from where it *would* be; also anchors absolute children.
- `position: absolute` — remove from flow; place against the nearest positioned ancestor with top/right/bottom/left.
- `position: fixed` — pin to the viewport (classic sticky header).
- `position: sticky` — scrolls normally, then sticks at a threshold.

Use positioning for overlays, badges and pinned bars — not for general page layout. Layout is flexbox and grid's job (next lessons).

keyTakeaways: content → padding → border → margin, inside out.
Set box-sizing: border-box globally, always.
Positioning is for overlays and pinning; flex/grid do layout.

sections.heading: Turn it on
sections.body: Set `display: flex` on a **container** and its direct children become **flex items** laid out along a main axis (row by default):

sections.heading: The two axes
sections.body: `flex-direction: row` → main axis is horizontal, cross axis vertical. `flex-direction: column` flips them. **justify-content** distributes along the main axis (`flex-start`, `center`, `space-between`, `space-around`); **align-items** aligns along the cross axis (`stretch`, `center`, `flex-start`, `flex-end`). Memorize: *justify = main, align = cross*.

sections.heading: Growing and shrinking
sections.body: Items can flex: `flex: 1` makes an item absorb available space. A classic pattern — logo left, links pushed right:

sections.heading: Wrapping
sections.body: `flex-wrap: wrap` lets items flow to the next line instead of squishing — combined with `gap`, it's an instant responsive tag/chip layout.

keyTakeaways: display: flex on the parent; children become flex items.
justify-content = main axis, align-items = cross axis.
flex: 1 and margin-left: auto are the two most useful spacing tricks.

sections.body: `fr` means a *fraction of free space*. `grid-template-columns: 2fr 1fr` gives the first column twice the width of the second. Mix with fixed sizes: `240px 1fr` is a classic sidebar + content.

sections.heading: Flex or grid?
sections.body: Rule of thumb: **flexbox** for a line of things (navbars, button rows, centering); **grid** for two-dimensional arrangements (galleries, dashboards, page skeletons). They nest happily — a grid page with flex components inside is the norm.

lessons.title: Media queries, fluid units and mobile-first

content.objective: Make one codebase look right from a phone to a desktop monitor.

sections.heading: Mobile-first thinking
sections.body: Write your base styles for small screens, then *add* complexity as space grows. This keeps CSS additive instead of full of overrides:

sections.heading: Relative units
sections.body:
- `rem` — relative to the root font size (16px default). Use for font sizes, padding, widths: respects user font settings.
- `%` — relative to the parent. Good for fluid widths.
- `vw`/`vh` — percent of the viewport. `100vh` = full screen height.

Avoid fixed px font sizes; `1rem` body text scales with user preferences.

rem for sizing, clamp() for fluid type, max-width: 100% for images.

sections.heading: let and const
sections.body: `const` declares a value that won't be reassigned; `let` declares one that will. Default to const — reach for let only when reassignment is the point. (You'll see `var` in old code; treat it as legacy.)

sections.heading: Strings and template literals
sections.body: Backtick strings interpolate values with ${} — vastly nicer than + concatenation:

sections.heading: Comparison: always ===
sections.body: `===` compares value *and* type; `==` performs sneaky type conversion first (`"5" == 5` is true!). Always use === and !== — this single habit prevents a whole category of bugs.

keyTakeaways: const by default, let when reassigning, never var.
Core types: string, number, boolean, undefined, null.
Template literals `${...}` for building strings; === for comparing.

content.objective: Branch with if/else and repeat with loops — the control flow of every program.

sections.heading: Truthy and falsy
sections.body: In a condition, JavaScript converts any value to a boolean. Exactly six values are **falsy**: `false`, `0`, `""` (empty string), `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`. Everything else is truthy — including `"0"` and empty arrays. This enables concise checks like `if (username) { ... }` for 'is it non-empty'.

sections.heading: Logical operators
sections.body: `&&` (and), `||` (or), `!` (not). `||` also provides defaults: `const name = input || "Anonymous"`. The newer `??` only falls back on null/undefined, which is safer when 0 or "" are valid values.

sections.heading: switch for many exact cases
sections.body: When comparing one value against many exact options, switch reads cleaner than an else-if ladder — just don't forget the break statements.

keyTakeaways: Six falsy values: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN.
for...of is the everyday loop for arrays.
?? falls back only on null/undefined; || falls back on any falsy value.

sections.heading: return vs console.log
sections.body: A common beginner trap: `console.log` *shows* a value; `return` *hands it back* to the caller so it can be stored or passed on. A function without return gives back undefined. Log to inspect; return to produce.

sections.heading: Scope: who can see what
sections.body: Variables declared inside a function (or any {} block, for let/const) exist only there. Inner scopes can read outer variables; outer scopes cannot see in. This containment is a feature — it prevents unrelated code from stepping on your variables.

sections.heading: Functions as values
sections.body: Functions can be stored in variables and handed to other functions. This is the door to everything modern: array methods, event handlers, React props all pass functions around.

keyTakeaways: Arrow functions are the everyday form; implicit return for one-liners.
return produces a value; console.log only displays one.
Inner scopes see outward; nothing sees inward.

sections.body: Handlers receive an event object describing what happened. Two members you'll use constantly: `event.target` (the element that triggered it) and `event.preventDefault()` (stop the browser's default action — essential for forms):

content.objective: Understand why async exists and read/write async/await fluently.

sections.heading: Why async exists
sections.body: JavaScript runs on one thread — it does one thing at a time. If fetching data from a server took 2 seconds *synchronously*, the entire page would freeze: no clicks, no scrolling. So slow operations (network, timers) are **asynchronous**: JS starts them, moves on, and comes back when the result arrives.

sections.heading: Promises
sections.body: A Promise is a placeholder for a future value. It's *pending*, then either *fulfilled* (with a value) or *rejected* (with an error):

sections.heading: async/await: promises that read like normal code
sections.body: Inside an `async` function, `await` pauses that function (not the page!) until a promise settles:

sections.heading: Handling failure
sections.body: Awaited rejections become throwable errors — catch them with the try/catch you'd use anywhere:

sections.heading: The execution order intuition
sections.body: Test yourself: `console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0); console.log(3);` prints **1, 3, 2** — even with a 0ms delay. Async callbacks always wait until current synchronous code finishes. Internalize this and half of all async confusion disappears.

keyTakeaways: Async keeps the single thread free; the page never freezes waiting.
await pauses the async function, not the program.
try/catch/finally around await is the standard error pattern.

content.objective: Request JSON data from a server and handle every outcome: success, HTTP error, network failure.

sections.heading: The gotcha everyone hits
sections.body: fetch only rejects on *network* failure (offline, DNS). A 404 or 500 response resolves normally — you must check `response.ok` yourself. Skipping that check is the most common fetch bug in existence.

sections.heading: The three UI states
sections.body: Every data-driven interface has exactly three states, and users must see all of them: **loading** (show a spinner or message), **success** (show the data), **error** (show what went wrong). Structure code around them:

keyTakeaways: Always check response.ok — HTTP errors don't throw on their own.
response.json() is itself async: await it.
Design for three states: loading, success, error.

sections.heading: ES Modules
sections.body: Real projects split code into files that import each other:

sections.heading: Enabling modules in the browser
sections.body: One attribute change: `<script type="module" src="app.js">`. Module scripts get their own scope (no accidental globals) and defer automatically. Note: modules require a server (Live Server counts) — file:// URLs won't work.

sections.heading: Named vs default
sections.body: A file can have many **named exports** (imported with braces, exact names) and at most one **default export** (imported with any name, no braces). Convention: default-export the file's main thing, name-export helpers.

sections.heading: Patterns you'll see in every React file
sections.body: These four patterns appear in virtually every component — make them automatic now:

sections.heading: Why immutability matters already
sections.body: The update patterns above (spread-to-add, filter-to-remove, map-to-change) look ceremonial now — but React detects changes by comparing old and new references. Mutating an array in place makes changes invisible to React. Learn the patterns here, reap the benefit next stack.

keyTakeaways: type="module" unlocks import/export in the browser.
Braces for named imports; no braces for the default.
Immutable update patterns (spread/filter/map) are pre-work for React.

stacks.name: React

lessons.title: From render() calls to declarative UI

content.objective: Understand the problem React solves and the component mental model.

sections.heading: The problem you already felt
sections.body: In your JS capstone, every state change required you to remember to call render(), and render() rebuilt everything. Forget one call → stale screen. Rebuild too much → lost focus, flicker, wasted work. Keeping UI and state in sync *manually* is the core pain of frontend — and it grows brutally with app size.

sections.heading: React's deal
sections.body: React inverts the job: **you describe what the UI looks like for any given state; React updates the real DOM when state changes.** You never call render() or touch the DOM for updates. You declare; React reconciles. It compares the new description with the old one and applies only the minimal real-DOM changes needed.

sections.heading: Components: UI as functions
sections.body: A React component is literally a JavaScript function that returns a description of UI:

sections.heading: Composition: the app is a tree
sections.body: Apps are components made of components: App contains Header, ProductGrid, Footer; ProductGrid contains many ProductCards; each card contains a Button. Small, named, reusable pieces — the same instinct as extracting functions, applied to UI. Component names are Capitalized; that's how React tells them apart from HTML tags.

sections.heading: Where React runs
sections.body: React code uses JSX (next lesson) which browsers don't natively read, so projects use a build tool. Standard setup: `npm create vite@latest my-app` → choose React → `npm install` → `npm run dev`. The dev server rebuilds and refreshes on every save. Inside src/, App.jsx is your root component — everything you build hangs off it.

keyTakeaways: React's contract: you describe UI from state; it syncs the DOM.
Components are functions returning UI; apps are trees of them.
Vite is the standard way to scaffold and run a React project.

content.objective: Confirm the declarative model landed before writing code.

questions.prompt: In React, how does the screen get updated after data changes?
options: You edit the DOM with querySelector
React re-runs your components and applies minimal DOM changes
questions.explanation: That's the core contract: describe the UI, and React reconciles the DOM for you.

questions.prompt: What is a React component, mechanically?
options: A function that returns a UI description
questions.explanation: Components are plain functions (returning JSX) that React calls to know what to draw.

questions.prompt: Why must component names be capitalized?
options: So React can distinguish components from regular HTML tags
They must match the file name
questions.explanation: <welcomeBadge /> would be treated as an unknown HTML tag; <WelcomeBadge /> is your component.

questions.prompt: Which tool scaffolds and serves a React project during development?
questions.explanation: JSX needs a build step; Vite compiles it and hot-reloads the browser as you save.

content.objective: Write valid JSX and build reusable components that accept data.

sections.heading: JSX: HTML-shaped JavaScript
sections.body:
JSX looks like HTML but is JavaScript expressions. The differences that matter: 1. `className` instead of `class` (class is a reserved JS word). 2. Curly braces embed any JS expression: `{user.name}`, `{2 + 2}`, `{formatDate(d)}`. 3. A component returns **one** root element (wrap siblings in `<>...` — a Fragment). 4. Every tag closes — ``, ``, `
`.

sections.heading: Props: arguments for components
sections.body: Props make components reusable — same structure, different data. They arrive as a single object, almost always destructured in the parameter list:

sections.heading: Strings vs braces in props
sections.body: `name="Lamp"` passes a string. Everything else needs braces: `price={35}`, `inStock={false}`, `tags={["new", "sale"]}`, `onSelect={handleSelect}`. Passing `price="35"` (a string!) is a classic bug when you later compute with it.

sections.heading: Props flow down, and they're read-only
sections.body: Data flows parent → child. A component never modifies its own props — they're inputs, like function arguments. When data must change, that's *state* (next skill), and it lives in whichever component owns it.

sections.heading: The children prop
sections.body: Whatever you nest between a component's tags arrives as props.children — the pattern behind every layout/wrapper component:

keyTakeaways: className, one root, braces for expressions, close every tag.
Props = component inputs; destructure them, never mutate them.
Non-string props need braces: price={35}, not price="35".

sections.heading: What actually happens
sections.body: Calling setCount does two things: stores the new value, and tells React to **re-run the component function**. The function executes again, count now holds the new value, new JSX is returned, React diffs it and patches the DOM. That's the whole magic — state change → re-render → screen sync, automatically. (This is also why plain `count = count + 1` does nothing: no setter, no re-render.)

sections.heading: Events in React
sections.body: camelCase props holding functions: onClick, onChange, onSubmit. Pass the function — don't call it:

code.snippet:

<button onClick={handleSave()}>Save</button>         // ❌ called immediately
<button onClick={() => remove(item.id)}>×</button>   // ✅ arrow for arguments

sections.body: Your js-modern patterns become law here. React compares references — mutate in place and it sees 'same array, nothing changed':

sections.heading: State lives where it's shared
sections.body: Each component instance owns its state. When two components need the same data, the state moves **up** to their closest common parent and flows down as props — 'lifting state up'. The child asks for changes via a callback prop: `onToggle={handleToggle}`. Data down, events up: the fundamental React data flow.

keyTakeaways: setState stores the value AND triggers a re-render.
Pass handlers (onClick={fn}); wrap in an arrow to pass arguments.
Never mutate state; spread/filter/map to produce new values.
Shared state lifts up to the common parent; changes flow up via callbacks.

content.objective: Render dynamic lists with stable keys and show/hide UI cleanly.

sections.heading: Keys: identity for list items
sections.body: When rendering arrays, each element needs a `key` — a stable, unique identifier. React uses keys to match old and new list items during re-renders, preserving state and DOM correctly when items reorder, appear or vanish.

sections.heading: Why index-as-key backfires
sections.body: Using the array index works only for lists that never reorder or delete. Delete item 0 and every following item's index shifts — React now matches the wrong old/new pairs, and input values or checkbox states 'jump' between rows. Use real ids; generate one at creation time (crypto.randomUUID()) if the data has none.

sections.heading: Conditional rendering
sections.body: It's all just JavaScript expressions:

sections.heading: One trap with &&
sections.body: `{count && <Badge />}` renders the number 0 when count is 0 (0 is falsy but renderable!). Guard with a comparison: `{count > 0 && <Badge />}`.

keyTakeaways: Every mapped element needs a stable key — real ids, not indexes.
Ternary for either/or; && for maybe; early return for big branches.
Guard && with comparisons to avoid rendering a stray 0.

Derive visibleProducts by filtering on the query (case-insensitive) — no second state!

Storing filtered results in their own state is the classic 'two sources of truth' bug.

content.objective: Run side effects — like fetching — at the right moments, without infinite loops.

sections.heading: What's a side effect?
sections.body: Rendering should be pure: same props/state in, same JSX out. Anything that reaches outside — fetching data, timers, document.title, localStorage — is a **side effect** and gets its own home: useEffect.

sections.heading: The dependency array is the schedule
sections.body:
- `[]` — run once after the first render (mount). Initial data fetch lives here.
- `[a, b]` — run after mount AND whenever a or b changes.
- *(omitted)* — run after **every** render. Almost never what you want.

Setting state inside an effect with a missing/wrong dependency array is how infinite loops happen: render → effect → setState → render → effect → …

sections.heading: Fetching on mount: the full pattern
sections.body: All three UI states, in React form:

sections.heading: Cleanup
sections.body: Return a function from the effect to undo it — React calls it before re-running the effect and on unmount. Essential for timers and subscriptions:

sections.heading: Don't overuse effects
sections.body: If a value can be computed from existing props/state (like your filtered list), compute it during render — no effect, no extra state. Effects are for synchronizing with the *outside world*, not for reacting to your own state.

keyTakeaways: useEffect(fn, []) = run once on mount — home of the initial fetch.
Dependencies control re-runs; wrong deps cause loops or staleness.
Return a cleanup function for timers/subscriptions.
Derivable values don't need effects — compute them in render.
